questions.stem: Describe the Five Whys tool.
options: Ask why the symptom happens, then why that happens, about five times, until you reach a cause you could act on
Ask five people who know the work what they think the cause is, and take the answer that most of them agree on as the root cause
List five possible causes on the board and ask the team to vote for the one that seems most likely
Ask the customer five questions about the problem and build the diagnosis from their answers
questions.why: Five is a rule of thumb, not a law. See §3.1.

questions.stem: Explain where to stop in Five Whys.
options: At the last cause you could actually do something about
Exactly at the fifth why, because the method is designed to reach the root cause in five steps
When the answer is 'human nature', because that is the deepest cause any chain can reach
When the boss agrees with the answer, because a cause nobody accepts cannot be fixed
questions.why: 'Nobody owns the schedule' is fixable; 'people are careless' is giving up. See §3.1.

questions.stem: Identify the serious weakness of Five Whys.
options: It follows one chain, so the branch you happen to pick decides what you find
It is too slow for most business problems, because each why needs its own investigation
It needs expensive software to record the chain and the evidence behind each step
It cannot be used on service businesses, because it was developed for factory problems
questions.why: Asking a different first why leads somewhere else entirely. See §3.1.

questions.stem: Explain why 'people are careless' is not a cause.
options: You cannot do anything about it — it is giving up
It is too specific to be useful as a cause of a business problem
It is a symptom of the problem rather than a cause of it
It is a correlation, because careless people and problems appear together
questions.why: Stop at the last actionable cause. See §3.1.

questions.stem: Identify the evidence the café example uses for 'only one machine is running at peak'.
options: Observed
The maintenance log
A staff interview
Confirmed with finance
questions.why: Each why in the example names its evidence. See §3.1.

questions.stem: Describe a cause map.
options: The symptom on the left with every plausible cause branched, then branched again, with evidence marked beside each
A single chain of five whys drawn as a line from the symptom to the root cause, with the evidence for each link written at the end of the chain
A chart of complaint counts ordered from the largest to the smallest, with the cumulative share marked
A comparison of where the problem is and where it is not, laid out in two columns with the differences noted
questions.why: Slower than Five Whys and honest. See §3.2.

questions.stem: Identify the branch categories a cause map lists.
options: People, process, equipment, materials, information
Price, product, place, promotion, people
Price, product, place, promotion and people
Boss, staff, customer, supplier, competitor
questions.why: List every branch without arguing about which is right. See §3.2.

questions.stem: Explain what a branch with no evidence behind it is.
options: A hypothesis, not a cause — label it as one out loud
A proven cause, because it appears on the map alongside the others
A symptom that has been placed on the wrong side of the map
A decoy added to make the map look more complete than it is
questions.why: It is the fastest way to be taken seriously. See §3.2.

questions.stem: Explain what fifteen branches on a cause map usually means.
options: You are listing symptoms again rather than causes
The problem is very serious and has many independent causes
The map is excellent, because nothing has been missed
You need more branches, because fifteen is still too few
questions.why: Five branches is usually enough. See §3.2.

questions.stem: Explain what to do after marking the evidence beside each branch.
options: Test the branches with no evidence instead of believing them
Pick the branch the client likes most, because the project needs support
Delete the branches with no evidence so that the map shows only facts
Stop — the map is finished once the evidence has been marked
questions.why: Hypotheses are tested, not believed. See §3.2.

questions.stem: Describe the IS / IS NOT tool.
options: Ask where the problem IS and where it IS NOT, then look for what is different between them
Ask why five times until you reach the cause you can act on
Count the complaints and rank them from the largest share to the smallest
List every possible cause on a map and mark the evidence beside each one
questions.why: It rules causes out faster than proving one in. See §3.3.

questions.stem: Identify the four questions in an IS / IS NOT table.
options: What? Where? When? Who?
Why? How? How much? How long?
Cost? Speed? Quality? Risk?
Mess? Symptom? Problem? Plan?
questions.why: Four rows: what, where, when, who. See §3.3.

questions.stem: Explain what IS / IS NOT does for you.
options: It rules causes OUT, which is faster than proving one in
It proves the cause by showing exactly where the problem comes from
It counts the damage each cause is doing to the business
It finds the budget needed to fix the problem in each location
questions.why: If five branches are fine, chain-wide causes are eliminated. See §3.3.

questions.stem: Identify the column to fill first in an IS / IS NOT table, and the reason.
options: The IS NOT column — students find it harder, and it is where the value is
The IS column — it is easier and gives the team confidence to continue
The difference column — it holds the answer, so it should be written first
Any column — the order makes no difference to the result
questions.why: Fill IS NOT first. See §3.3.

questions.stem: Identify the method IS / IS NOT comes from.
options: Kepner-Tregoe
Toyota
Toyota's production system
Kahneman
questions.why: From the Kepner-Tregoe method. See §3.3.

questions.stem: Describe the Pareto rule.
options: A small number of causes produce most of the damage, so count them and put them in order before you spend
All causes are equal, so the budget should be divided evenly between them
The cheapest cause should be fixed first, so that the budget goes further
Fix every cause at once, because leaving any cause untouched lets the problem return
questions.why: Typically 80/20. See §3.4.

questions.stem: Identify the share of complaints the top two causes carry in the chapter's table.
questions.why: Waiting (46%) + order wrong (28%) = 74%. See §3.4.

questions.stem: Explain why fixing 'staff attitude' first would be a mistake in the chapter's table.
options: It addresses one complaint in eight while two causes carry 74%
Staff attitude cannot be fixed, because it depends on personality
It is the biggest cause, so it should be left until the budget is larger
Customers do not mention attitude, so it does not appear in the table
questions.why: 12% of complaints. Count before you choose. See §3.4.

questions.stem: Explain why rough counts are still worth doing.
options: A rough order is far better than an argument about impressions
Rough counts are always exact enough to publish in the final report
Counting is required by law before any money is spent on a fix
Counting replaces evidence, so once the counts are done nothing else is needed
questions.why: Do the counting even when the numbers are rough. See §3.4.

questions.stem: Describe when Pareto comes in the diagnosis sequence.
options: Last, when you must choose what to fix
First, before any other tool, so that the team knows where to look
Instead of a cause map, because it does the same job with numbers
Only in finance, where the damage can be measured in money
questions.why: Pareto comes last. See §3.4 and §3.6.

questions.stem: Describe a guess.
options: It sounds right and no evidence supports it yet — legitimate as a hypothesis, not as a finding
Two things moving together over the same period, which suggests but does not prove a link
A cause with a mechanism that explains it and evidence that survives the IS NOT test
A proven fact that the client has confirmed from their own experience of running the business for many years
questions.why: Illegitimate the moment you present it as a finding. See §3.5.

questions.stem: Describe a correlation.
options: Two things move together — a clue, not proof
A proven cause, because the two things always appear together
A guess with no evidence behind it at all
A symptom of the problem rather than a cause of it
questions.why: Sales fell when the clinic opened: a clue, not a cause. See §3.5.

questions.stem: Describe a cause, as the chapter defines it.
options: You can explain the mechanism, the evidence survives the IS NOT test, and when it was removed the problem changed
Two things that happen together often enough for the pattern to be noticed by the staff
Something the client believes strongly enough to have acted on it before the project began
The first why in a Five Whys chain, which points directly at the visible symptom
questions.why: Best of all: removing it changed the problem. See §3.5.

questions.stem: Identify the question to ask before every claim about a cause.
options: 'What would I expect to see if this were NOT the cause?'
'Will the client like this answer when they see it in the report?'
'How much would it cost to fix this if it turns out to be the cause?'
'Who in the organisation is to blame for letting this happen?'
questions.why: If the answer is 'the same thing', you have a guess. See §3.5.

questions.stem: Explain what it means if you would 'see the same thing' whether or not X is the cause.
options: You have a guess
You have a cause
You have a correlation
You have a symptom
questions.why: Same observation either way = guess. See §3.5.

questions.stem: Identify the tool for one clear symptom with probably one chain.
options: Five Whys
Cause map
IS / IS NOT
Pareto
questions.why: Fast, and enough when the chain really is a chain. See §3.6.

questions.stem: Identify the tool when several things could be causing the problem.
options: Cause map
Five Whys
Pareto
A staff survey
questions.why: Holds competing causes without choosing early. See §3.6.

questions.stem: Identify the tool when the problem happens here but not there.
options: IS / IS NOT
Five Whys
Pareto
Cause map or Five Whys
questions.why: Comparison rules causes out. See §3.6.

questions.stem: Identify the tool for many causes and a limited budget.
options: Pareto
IS / IS NOT
Five Whys
Cause map
questions.why: Puts them in order so you spend where the damage is. See §3.6.

questions.stem: Describe the two-tool combination used in practice.
options: A cause map or Five Whys to get candidates, then IS / IS NOT to eliminate most of them
Pareto to rank the causes, then Five Whys on the largest one
Two cause maps built by different teams and compared
IS / IS NOT to find the differences, then a survey to confirm them
questions.why: Pareto comes last, when you must choose. See §3.6.

questions.stem: Describe what the 'When?' row points to if the problem started in March.
options: Something that changed in March
Something about the product that has always been there
Something local to one branch and its layout
The staff on shift at the time the problem occurs
questions.why: When? → something that changed at that time. See §3.3.

questions.stem: Explain why the cause map is called 'honest'.
options: It shows every plausible cause and which ones actually have evidence
It is quick to build, so there is no temptation to leave anything out
It only shows the right answer once the evidence has been collected
It never changes once it has been drawn and agreed with the client
questions.why: Most branches will have no evidence — that is the finding. See §3.2.

questions.stem: Analyse the chain: slow coffee → one machine at peak → second machine broken → not serviced → nobody owns the schedule → no maintenance budget line. Determine the best stopping point.
options: 'Nobody owns the service schedule' — fixable on Monday
'People are careless' — the deepest cause the chain can reach
'The economy' — the reason there is no maintenance budget
'Customers are impatient' — the reason the slow coffee is noticed
questions.why: Stop at the last cause you could do something about. See §3.1.

questions.stem: Analyse a Five Whys chain that ends at 'human nature'. Determine the error.
options: It went one why too far — the end point is true and useless
It stopped too early, before the real cause was reached
It used the wrong first why, so the whole chain was misdirected
It needs a sixth why to reach the cause that can be acted on
questions.why: Every chain ends at human nature if you go too far. See §3.1 and the opening questions.

questions.stem: Analyse a 22-minute prescription wait. Determine what Five Whys might miss.
options: A cause on a different chain, such as stock or rota, because it follows one chain
Nothing — it finds everything if the whys are asked carefully
The symptom, because Five Whys starts from the cause
The budget, because Five Whys does not consider cost
questions.why: Five Whys follows one chain. See §3.1 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Classify the step 'because it was not serviced for nine months — maintenance log'.
options: A why resting on evidence
A why resting on assumption
A guess
A correlation
questions.why: The example marks which steps rest on evidence. See §3.1.

questions.stem: Determine what to do with a cause-map branch 'staff are poorly trained' that has no evidence.
options: Label it a hypothesis out loud and test it
Report it as the cause, because training problems are common
Delete it, because a branch with no evidence has no place on the map
Fix training immediately, because the cost of being wrong is low
questions.why: A branch with no evidence is a hypothesis. See §3.2.

questions.stem: Analyse a cause map of the pharmacy wait with branches: rota, stock system, counter layout, prescription complexity. Determine what the map adds over Five Whys.
options: It holds several competing causes at once instead of the one chain you picked first
Nothing — both tools find the same causes in the end
A count of complaints under each branch, which Five Whys cannot provide
A comparison with other branches, which shows where the problem is not
questions.why: Holds competing causes without choosing early. See §3.2 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Select the correct response when a client asks 'so which branch is the cause?' before any evidence exists.
options: 'These are hypotheses — here is how we will test each one'
'This one — it feels right, and experience counts for a lot in this business'
'All of them — each branch contributes something to the problem'
'We cannot know — causes can never be proved in a service business'
questions.why: Label hypotheses as such in front of the client. See §3.2.

questions.stem: Analyse the food delivery case: late orders in two of nine zones, dinner only, since February, restaurants only. Determine the fact that eliminates most causes.
options: Only two of nine zones — anything company-wide (app, pay rate, customer base) is eliminated
Dinner orders only — anything to do with the lunchtime menu is eliminated
Since February — anything that was true before February is eliminated
Restaurants only — anything to do with grocery partners is eliminated
questions.why: Two zones rule out every chain-wide cause. See Exercise 2 and §3.3.

questions.stem: Determine what 'dinner orders, not lunch' points to in the delivery case.
options: Something about evening conditions — traffic, rider numbers or restaurant prep at dinner
The app, which may be slower under the heavier load of the evening
Rider pay, which is lower in the evening than at lunch
The customer base, which is different in the evening
questions.why: When? → what is different at that time. See §3.3.

questions.stem: Determine what 'restaurants, not grocery partners' points to.
options: Something about restaurant preparation or pickup, not the delivery system as a whole
The riders, who prefer grocery orders because they are quicker
The two zones' roads, which are congested near restaurants
The customers, who order from restaurants at busier times
questions.why: What? → something about that order type. See §3.3.

questions.stem: Analyse the Deira coffee case: 7–9 a.m. only, Deira only, coffee only, morning shift only. Determine a cause that is eliminated.
options: A chain-wide coffee bean problem — the other five branches are fine
A morning rota problem at the Deira branch
Something that changed in March at the Deira branch
A Deira-specific machine that struggles in the morning
questions.why: Causes that apply to the whole chain are eliminated. See §3.3.

questions.stem: Select the first data to ask for in the gym case (drop-out after a competitor opened and a timetable change).
options: Which classes the leavers attended and when they left, to compare against the timetable change
The competitor's prices, so that the gym can match them
The gym's logo and brand image compared with the competitor's
Staff opinions about why the members have been leaving
questions.why: Build the IS / IS NOT; ask for the data that settles the difference. See Exercise 3 and §3.3.

questions.stem: Analyse a Pareto table: waiting 46%, order wrong 28%, attitude 12%, price 8%. Determine where to spend first with budget for two fixes.
options: Waiting and order wrong — 74% of complaints
Attitude and price — the two causes that are cheapest to fix
Price and other — the two causes the owner mentioned first
Attitude and waiting — the two causes customers mention most loudly
questions.why: Count before you choose. See §3.4.

questions.stem: Analyse a manager with eleven causes and budget for two who picks 'the easiest two'. Determine the chapter's view.
options: Wrong basis — choose by the share of damage each cause carries
Correct — easy wins first build the momentum the team needs for the harder fixes later
Correct — cost matters most when the budget is limited
It depends on the boss, who decides how the budget is spent
questions.why: Pareto: order by damage, then spend. See §3.4 and the opening questions.

questions.stem: Determine the share of complaints left after fixing the top two causes in the chapter's table.
Classify 'member drop-out rose after the competitor opened in March'.
options: A correlation — two things moved together
A cause — the competitor took the members
A guess — nothing supports the link
A symptom only — the drop-out is the visible sign
questions.why: Moving together is a clue, not proof. See §3.5 and Exercise 3.

questions.stem: Classify 'our members clearly left for the cheaper gym'.
options: A guess — no evidence supports it yet
A cause — the mechanism is obvious
A correlation — members left when the gym opened
A finding — the consultant has looked at the evidence
questions.why: It sounds right and nothing supports it. See §3.5.

questions.stem: Analyse the gym footnote: timetable changed in February and 60% of leavers attended classes. Determine the effect on the consultant's claim.
options: It offers a rival cause the IS NOT test must settle before the price is cut
It confirms the competitor caused it, because the leavers were the most active members
It is irrelevant, because the timetable change happened before the competitor opened
It proves price is the cause, because class members are the most price-sensitive
questions.why: What would you see if the competitor were NOT the cause? See §3.5.

questions.stem: Determine when a correlation may be called a cause.
options: When you can explain the mechanism, it survives the IS NOT test, and removing it changed the problem
When the client agrees that it is the most likely explanation
When it has happened twice in the same way
When it is written in a report with the data behind it
questions.why: Three conditions for a cause. See §3.5.

questions.stem: Analyse 'ice cream sales and drowning both rise in July'. Determine the lesson for business data.
options: Things that move together may share a third cause, such as the season
Ice cream causes drowning, because people swim too soon after eating it in the heat
Correlation always equals cause when the data is strong enough
July is dangerous, so businesses should plan for it
questions.why: A third thing causes both. See §3.5 and the opening questions.

questions.stem: Select the tool for 'late deliveries happen in two zones but not the other seven'.
options: IS / IS NOT
Five Whys
Pareto
A cause map only
questions.why: The problem happens here but not there. See §3.6.

questions.stem: Select the tool for 'complaints come from many causes and we can fix two'.
options: Pareto
Five Whys
IS / IS NOT
Assumption reversal
questions.why: Many causes, limited budget. See §3.6.

questions.stem: Select the tool for 'one clear symptom: the second coffee machine keeps breaking'.
options: Five Whys
Pareto
IS / IS NOT
A survey
questions.why: One clear symptom, probably one chain. See §3.6.

questions.stem: Determine the order of tools for a project diagnosis session.
options: Cause map or Five Whys for candidates → IS / IS NOT to eliminate → Pareto to choose
Pareto to rank the causes → Five Whys on the largest → cause map to check
IS / IS NOT to find the differences → Pareto to rank → Five Whys to explain
Any order — the tools are independent and give the same result
questions.why: In practice you use two, then Pareto last. See §3.6.

questions.stem: Analyse a group that argues about the right cause while building the cause map. Determine the error.
options: They stopped to argue instead of listing every branch first
They listed too many branches, which made the map impossible to use
They used Five Whys when the cause map was the right tool
They counted complaints before the branches were complete
questions.why: Do not stop to argue about which is right. See §3.2.

questions.stem: Determine what to tell a client about your leading cause when you only have a correlation.
options: Say honestly it is a correlation and name the test that would settle it
Call it the cause, because the client needs a clear answer
Say nothing until the evidence is complete
Call it a guess, because nothing has been proved
questions.why: Say which of the three you are holding. See §3.5.

questions.stem: Analyse a table where IS and IS NOT are identical for every row. Determine what it tells you.
options: The comparison rules nothing out — you need a different comparison or more data
The cause is found, because the problem is the same everywhere
The problem is everywhere, so nothing can be done about it
Pareto is needed, because the differences must be counted
questions.why: The value is in the differences. See §3.3.

questions.stem: Determine why a Five Whys chain should mark each step 'evidence' or 'assumption'.
options: So you know which links are proven and which are still hypotheses
To make the chain longer and more convincing in the report
Because the client asks for the evidence behind each step before approving the fix
To replace the cause map, which does the same job
questions.why: Mark which rest on evidence and which on assumption. See §3.1 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Analyse a manager who says 'I feel most complaints are about staff'. Determine the chapter's response.
options: Count them — a rough order beats an argument about impressions
Trust the feeling, because the manager knows the business better than anyone else
Fix staff first, because the manager is probably right
Ignore complaints, because they are only impressions
questions.why: Do the counting even when rough. See §3.4.

questions.stem: Analyse a diagnosis that used only a survey of staff opinions. Determine the weakness.
options: Opinions are hypotheses; no tool ruled causes out or ordered them
Surveys are always wrong, because staff protect themselves and their colleagues
Staff never know the cause of the problems they work with
It needs more opinions before a conclusion can be drawn
questions.why: Evidence and elimination, not impressions. See §3.2, §3.3 and §3.6.

questions.stem: Select the statement that is a cause rather than a correlation.
options: 'Removing the broken machine from the rota cut the queue in half the next day'
'Queues rose when the new clinic opened across the road in March'
'Busy days have longer queues than quiet days at every branch'
'Customers say the staff are slow and do not seem to care'
questions.why: Removed it, and the problem changed. See §3.5.

questions.stem: Classify a decision to fix the cause with 8% of complaints because it is cheapest.
options: Spending where the damage is not — Pareto says order by damage first
Good Pareto practice — the cheapest fix always gives the best return on the budget
An IS / IS NOT result — the cause was found by comparison
A Five Whys result — the chain ended at the cheapest cause
questions.why: Fixing the small cause first addresses one complaint in twelve. See §3.4.
